newsitem.title: USA: State issues cease and desist order against Kevorkian.
newsitem.headline: State issues cease and desist order against Kevorkian.

text.p: Michigan regulators threatened Dr. Jack Kevorkian with jail Friday if he did not stop practicing medicine without a license, prompting the assisted suicide advocate to burn the order in front of TV cameras.

"That is not I burning that paper," Kevorkian proclaimed outside of a state building in downtown Detroit. "That is the patients I've helped and the suffering humanity that have been insulted by this despicable gesture."
Kevorkian and his attorney Geoffrey Fieger said they received the "cease and desist order" Friday morning from the Michigan Department of Consumer and Industry Services.

The action warned the 68-year-old retired pathologist he could face four years in jail and a fine of $2,000 if he is found to be practicing medicine without a license, a felony. Kevorkian's medical license was suspended in 1992.

It was the strongest action state officials have taken against Kevorkian since legislators passed a temporary law banning doctor-assisted suicide four years ago. That law expired in 1994, and county prosecutors have failed on three attempts to put Kevorkian behind bars for helping people die.

"If Kevorkian choses to ignore the cease and desist order, we then are able through the attorney general to go into circuit court and start procedings on our own criminal case," said Kathy Wilbur, director of the state department.

Fieger blasted the order as "incomprehensible, unbelievable, tyrannical, unacceptable." As he has in the past, Fieger unleashed a personal attack on Michigan Gov. John Engler, calling him "fat" and "ugly" and accusing him of orchestrating the action.
"The person behind this is John 'Nutcase' Engler, and he is following the dictates of his puppet masters, the religious right," said Fieger.
After setting fire to the order, Kevorkian made a brief statement saying he has a moral duty to disobey immoral laws. He then left with Fieger and several other associates without taking questions.

Kevorkian, who said he acts to relieve suffering, has acknowledged being present at 45 suicides since 1990. But he has not acknowledged any connection to five people who have killed themselves since February.
The bodies of one of those people was found in Kevorkian's van. Three of them left notes referring authorities to Fieger, who was their attorney.

The order issued Friday only applied to violations Kevorkian is found to have committed after Friday, said Wilbur. It did not cover the order barring him from obtaining controlled substances, or the state's unwritten "common law" ban on assisted suicide.

Because Kevorkian has not admitted any involvement with a patient since last year, Wilbur acknowledged it could be difficult to prove he was practicing without a license by meeting, diagnosing and treating patients.
Kevorkian was scheduled to stand trial in Ionia, Mich., in June on assisted suicide charges for his role in the Aug. 30, 1996 death of 54-year-old Loretta Peabody.
